title: Writing the Test That Catches It

questions.question: What is the question to ask of every check you write?
options: What would have to be wrong for this to fail
Does this cover a line that was not covered
Is this the fastest way to assert it
Does this match the implementation
questions.explanation: If the answer is nothing you can think of, the check could never have failed and is not a test. Matching the implementation is the subtler version of the same problem: the check follows the code wherever it goes, including into a bug.

questions.question: A checks_pass that simply returns false rejects all six broken implementations. Why is that not a solution?
options: It also rejects the correct one, and a suite that rejects correct code is worse than no suite
It is too slow
It does not report which implementation failed
It would pass, but for the wrong reason
questions.explanation: The next real failure is not believed, because the suite has taught everybody that a red result means the test is wrong. A suite is judged from both sides at once.

questions.question: One implementation is wrong only when the remaining distance equals the step size exactly. What finds it?
options: A check that asks for that case by name, since sampling lands on a single point with probability near zero
A loop over a hundred evenly spaced starting positions
Random input generation, given enough runs
A check that the step is never exceeded
questions.explanation: Measured: the hundred and one position sweep misses it, and so does every other property in the suite. Only the two checks written for that boundary catch it.

questions.question: Where do the boundaries worth testing come from?
options: Every comparison in the implementation decides something, and each produces three cases: below, exactly, and above
The extremes of the input type
Whatever the coverage report highlights
The values in the specification's examples
questions.explanation: Two of the three are usually obvious and the third is the one that ships. The cheap habit is that whenever a test uses a value near a limit, add one at the limit.

questions.question: A suite written entirely with the target above the current value misses which fault?
options: A limiter that only ever adds, which runs away from any target below it
A limiter that does not limit
A limiter that will not stay where it arrived
A limiter that ignores a step of zero
questions.explanation: Direction is a dimension of the input that is easy not to notice, because the first example anybody writes moves upward and every one after it is copied from that.

questions.question: Two checks in this lesson each catch only the same single fault. Are they redundant?
options: Given these six implementations, yes, and a seventh that broke one direction and not the other would separate them
Yes, and one should be deleted
No, redundancy is impossible in a test suite
No, because they exercise different lines
questions.explanation: Removing a check and finding nothing slips through says it is redundant against the faults you have, not that it is worthless. A check that catches no fault at all is the one to question.
